newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK INTERBAK RATES JUMP AS LIQUIDITY TIGHTENS.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK INTERBAK RATES JUMP AS LIQUIDITY TIGHTENS.

text.p: Slovak interbank rates soared on Thursday amid money market liquidity shortage and dealers predict no significant downtrend in the near future.
Short-term rates jumped to around 35 percent from Wednesday's close of 24 percent. Longer maturities, which traded thinly, put one-month money at 35 percent.
Dealers said the main reason behind rate rises was a growing budget deficit which forced the finance ministry to accept high yields in auctions of state securities.
"There is no reason why rates should fall in foreseeable future," said Rastislav Zivor of ING Bank.
"The state is accepting high yields (in T-bill and state bond auctions) and this drains any possible excessive liquidity from the market," he added.

Average yield in a Slovak finance ministry auction of 13-week treasury bills rose to 18.248 percent on Wednesday, from 14.84 percent in the last successful auction of T-bills with similar maturity on April 9.
Budget deficit, covered mainly by T-bills and state bonds, widened to 17.790 billion crowns as of July 8, 1997, from 7.177 billion crowns in the January-May period of 1997.
"The market is paralysed at the moment because everything goes to high-yielding state securities," said Dalibor Cernicka of Bratislava-based Money Market Brokers.

"Another strong factor that is likely to keep rates up is very strong demand for crown funds from foreign banks," he said, adding that it seemed "as if foreign players were trying to prepare crown positions to repeat their pressure on the currency.
Cernicka expected rates for all maturities to stay above 30 percent in longer-term.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) faced strong downward pressure on the crown in May and June and its main tool to defend the currency was a radical squeeze of the money market liquidity to limit access to crown funds.

The central bank appears to have won the first battle for currency stability, but many analysts have said the crown remained very vulnerable and was still a target for further attacks due to the country's weak foreign trade position.
